Reproductive Health

About spaying and neutering cats.

1

1. Hormones and the feline reproductive cycle

A cat's reproductive cycle depends on the season and the amount of daylight. In the Northern Hemisphere, cats are most active in spring and summer, when days are long. From October to December comes a resting period — anestrus — when sex hormone (estrogen) levels drop to a minimum. However, in cats living indoors under artificial lighting (around 14 hours of light per day), this cycle can run year-round regardless of season.

A cat's cycle consists of several stages, each with its own hormones, behaviors, and physical changes.

Proestrus (preparation for heat) lasts a very short time, usually less than a day: the body begins producing estrogen in preparation for possible mating. The cat becomes very affectionate and rubs against objects, but doesn't yet allow males near her.

Estrus (heat itself) is the period when the cat is ready to mate. It lasts from 2 to 19 days (about a week on average). Eggs mature in the ovaries and hormone levels rise sharply, which changes the cat's behavior: she adopts a distinctive posture (arching her back and holding her tail to the side), meows loudly, rolls on the floor, and eats less. Owners who haven't seen this before sometimes think the cat is sick or in pain.

Veterinary medicine also recognizes other variations of heat: “split heat” — when signs begin, fade for a couple of days, and then return again (common in young cats); prolonged heat — when heat lasts longer than a week (common in Siamese cats), which can be linked to hormonal cysts on the ovaries.

If fertilization doesn't occur, interestrus (the interval between heat cycles) follows, lasting about a week — hormone levels drop, but new follicles immediately begin maturing, so the lull doesn't last long and the exhausting cycle starts all over again.

2

2. The mystery of ovulation: what triggers it

For a long time it was believed that cats could only become pregnant as a result of mechanical stimulation during mating — this is triggered by microscopic barbs on the male cat's penis, which set off the necessary nerve reflex.

However, modern research has shown that in more than 30% of cats, ovulation can occur spontaneously — without any male involvement at all. This process can be triggered by the scent of a male, the presence of other cats in heat nearby, or even simply a person petting the cat's back and lower back.

The main problem with spontaneous ovulation is that if the cat doesn't become pregnant, her body still begins preparing for motherhood (a false pregnancy sets in, lasting up to 50 days). During this time the uterus is exposed for a prolonged period to the hormone progesterone — this protects against new heat cycles but significantly raises the risk of serious infections and uterine cysts.

Pregnancy in cats lasts about two months (65-66 days on average). Labor itself takes anywhere from 4 to 42 hours. Cats are very fertile: a litter usually contains 1 to 5 kittens, and the probability of becoming pregnant after mating is very high — almost 74%.

3

3. The male reproductive system

For a population to grow this quickly, male cats need to be active too. Sexual maturity in male cats comes with rising testosterone, which is what causes those barbs to develop on the penis, stimulating the female.

Veterinarians advise not allowing male cats to breed before they reach one year of age, so their bodies are fully developed and their sperm is of good quality. Male cats' reproductive capability lasts until 10-12 years of age, though semen quality declines with age.

If a male cat is infertile or has health problems, mating still triggers ovulation in the female, but pregnancy doesn't occur — as a result, the female suffers from a false pregnancy, and her risk of uterine disease increases. In addition, unneutered male cats often mark territory, are aggressive toward other animals, and need to be kept isolated.

4

4. How the population grows: facts and myths

There are a lot of myths surrounding cat reproduction. The most famous is the legend that a single pair of cats and their descendants can produce 420,000 kittens in just 7 years. In practice, this figure is impossible, since it assumes ideal conditions: 100% survival of every kitten, immediate maturation, and no disease or aging. If biological laws really worked that perfectly, a single city would produce 76 billion cats in 10 years.

Realistic scientific calculations account for the high mortality rate on the streets: about 75% of stray kittens die within their first few months of life from infection, parasites, starvation, and vehicles. Factoring in this harsh reality, a pair of cats and their descendants over 7 years produce a much smaller, but still alarming, number — around 100 animals.

Modern computer models help calculate exactly how a population grows and how spaying/neutering affects it. If no measures are taken in a closed colony of 50 cats, roughly 1,000 kittens will be born and die from the hardships of life there over 10 years. Modeling shows that simple trapping and euthanasia don't work nearly as effectively as mass sterilization (TNR programs: Trap-Neuter-Return). Once the sterilization rate reaches the necessary threshold, the number of new kittens drops to zero, the population stabilizes, and then begins to decline.

5

5. The health and longevity benefits of spaying/neutering

Spaying/neutering doesn't just address the problem of homeless animals — it also protects the health of an individual pet. Large-scale medical studies show that neutered male cats live, on average, 62% longer than intact males, and spayed females live 39% longer than unspayed ones. This gap has a simple explanation: neutered animals are less likely to roam away from home, don't get into street fights (and therefore don't contract dangerous viruses like FIV or leukemia), and don't develop diseases of the reproductive system.

Pyometra (a pus-filled infection of the uterus) is a life-threatening condition in which the uterus fills with pus. It used to be thought that only dogs suffered from it, but cats are affected just as much, especially in middle and older age (around 7.5 years on average). The disease develops because of hormones: repeated false pregnancies cause the uterine lining to thicken and secrete large amounts of fluid, while local immunity drops, letting bacteria (often E. coli) easily get inside. Symptoms in cats are often hidden — discharge isn't always noticed, since cats are very meticulous about grooming themselves — instead, the animal becomes lethargic, refuses food, and may vomit. The main treatment is emergency surgery to remove the uterus and ovaries; if delayed, blood poisoning (sepsis) can set in. Routine, planned spaying completely eliminates the risk of this disease.

Mammary gland tumors are the third most common cancer in cats. Unlike in dogs, where about half of such tumors are benign, more than 90% of these growths in cats are malignant, growing very quickly and spreading to the lungs. The main driver of these tumors' growth is sex hormones released during heat cycles, so the best prevention is spaying at the right time.

Based on this evidence, veterinary organizations around the world have launched the “Fix by Five” campaign: it's recommended that kittens have their planned surgery strictly before they turn 5 months old. Myths claiming that early spaying/neutering harms growth or somehow narrows the urethra in male cats have long been disproven by science — surgery at a young age is much easier for animals to recover from, they wake from anesthesia faster, and shelters stop filling up with unwanted kittens.
